Cup of Blessing
KUP uv BLES-ing
noun phrase / doctrine
Cup (Old English cuppe, from Latin cuppa, tub or cask; by extension, the drinking vessel and its contents) + blessing (Old English blētsian, to consecrate by blood or to invoke divine favor). The phrase “cup of blessing” translates Greek to potērion tēs eulogías of 1 Corinthians 10:16, where Paul designates the Lord's Supper cup with the same term used in the Passover seder for the third cup of the Passover service — the cup drunk after the meal, over which a blessing was pronounced. The cup's Passover-seder background is the wine over which Jesus spoke the words of institution at the Last Supper (Luke 22:20: “This cup which is poured out for you is the new covenant in My blood”).

Biblical Definition

The cup of blessing is the consecrated cup of the Lord's Supper — the cup Paul identifies in 1 Corinthians 10:16 as “a sharing in the blood of Christ,” the vehicle through which the gathered church participates in the covenant sealed by Christ's poured-out blood. Paul's question is rhetorical: “Is not the cup of blessing which we bless a sharing in the blood of Christ?” The answer is yes — the cup genuinely participates in what it signifies and enacts, not in a Roman sacramental sense (transubstantiation), but in the Reformed sense that the Spirit genuinely feeds the faith of believing participants through the cup's enacted gospel-content. The cup of blessing at the Last Supper (Luke 22:20) is the Passover's third cup — the cup of redemption drunk after the Passover meal. Jesus takes this cup and identifies it with the new covenant in His blood: “This cup which is poured out for you is the new covenant in My blood.” Matthew 26:27–28 records His words of institution: “Drink from it, all of you. For this is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for forgiveness of sins.” The cup thus becomes the covenant-renewal instrument of the new covenant, the enacted proclamation of the shed blood that ratified the covenant at Calvary. Hebrews 9:20 quotes Exodus 24:8 (“This is the blood of the covenant”) in reference to the Mosaic covenant-inauguration at Sinai — establishing the typological lineage: Sinai blood on the people, cross blood in the cup. Every Supper cup carries this covenant-inaugurating weight.

Webster 1828 Definition

The cup of blessing is the consecrated Lord's Supper cup identified by Paul in 1 Corinthians 10:16 as a genuine sharing in Christ's blood — the enacted proclamation of the new covenant ratified by Christ's shed blood, rooted in the Passover seder's third cup and fulfilled in Jesus' words of institution at the Last Supper.

expand to see more

CUP OF BLESSING. Greek to potērion tēs eulogías (1 Cor 10:16): the consecrated cup of the Lord's Supper, over which a blessing is pronounced, identified by Paul as a genuine participation (koinōnia) in the blood of Christ.

2. Passover-seder background: the third of four Passover cups (“the cup of redemption” in rabbinic tradition), drunk after the Passover meal over which a blessing was pronounced. Jesus takes this cup at the Last Supper (Luke 22:20) and redefines its content: no longer the covenant blood of the Exodus redemption, but the new covenant blood of His own self-offering.

3. Words of institution (Matt 26:27–28): “Drink from it, all of you. For this is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for forgiveness of sins.” The cup is the new covenant's covenant-meal instrument, the blood of the covenant enacted in the drinking community.

4. The Reformed understanding: koinōnia (sharing/participation) in 1 Cor 10:16 is a real spiritual participation mediated by the Spirit through faith — not transubstantiation (the cup literally becomes blood) and not bare memorialism (the cup signifies nothing present); the Spirit genuinely feeds believing participants through the cup's enacted gospel-content.

5. Covenant-blood typology (Exod 24:8; Heb 9:20): Moses sprinkled blood on the people at Sinai saying “this is the blood of the covenant.” The cup of blessing is the new covenant's equivalent: Christ's blood applied to the covenant community not by sprinkling but by the cup's proclaiming and the faith's receiving.

Key Scripture

1 Cor 10:16 — "Is not the cup of blessing which we bless a sharing in the blood of Christ? Is not the bread which we break a sharing in the body of Christ?"

Matt 26:27 — "And when He had taken a cup and given thanks, He gave it to them, saying, “Drink from it, all of you."

Matt 26:28 — "For this is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for forgiveness of sins."

Luke 22:20 — "And in the same way He took the cup after they had eaten, saying, “This cup which is poured out for you is the new covenant in My blood."

Modern Corruption

The cup of blessing has been corrupted by Roman Catholic transubstantiation (the cup literally becomes Christ's blood through priestly consecration) and by Protestant sacramentarian memorialism (the cup is a bare symbol with no genuine spiritual participation in what it enacts) — both positions failing Paul's declared koinōnia (real participation) in 1 Corinthians 10:16.

expand to see more

Roman Catholic eucharistic theology teaches that through transubstantiation the cup's substance is converted into Christ's actual blood at the moment of priestly consecration. This position collapses the sign-and-thing-signified distinction that the Reformation recovered: the cup is the sign; the blood of Christ is the thing signified; the Spirit genuinely mediates the latter through the former to the faith of the believing participant, but the former does not literally become the latter. The Council of Trent anathematized the Reformed view; the Westminster Confession (29.6) and the 1689 LBCF (30.7) reject transubstantiation as repugnant to Scripture, overthrow the nature of the ordinance, and have been productive of much superstition.

The Zwinglian-sacramentarian reduction goes too far in the opposite direction: the cup is merely a memorial token, a symbol pointing to an absent Christ and his past work, with no genuine present participation mediated through it. First Corinthians 10:16 refuses this reduction: koinōnia in Paul's vocabulary is a genuine present sharing, not a commemorative gesture. The Reformed position (Calvin, the Westminster Standards, the 1689 LBCF) is that Christ is genuinely present to the faith of believers at the Supper through the Spirit's mediation — the cup is a genuine means of grace, not a mere memorial, even though Christ's body is in heaven and the cup contains wine.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The cup of blessing roots in the Passover seder's third cup (the cup of redemption), in Moses' covenant-blood-sprinkling at Sinai (Exod 24:8), in Christ's words of institution at the Last Supper, and in Paul's apostolic definition of the Supper cup as genuine koinōnia in the blood of Christ.

expand to see more

Passover seder third cup — “the cup of redemption”: the cup Jesus takes after the meal (Luke 22:20: “after they had eaten”) is the third Passover cup; its Exodus-redemption content is now reinterpreted by Jesus as the new-covenant blood ratification

Exodus 24:8 — covenant-blood typology: Moses sprinkles blood on the people at Sinai declaring “this is the blood of the covenant”; Jesus echoes this formula exactly at the Last Supper (Matt 26:28: “this is my blood of the covenant”), establishing the new covenant's blood-ratification in fulfillment of the old

Matthew 26:27–28 — words of institution: the cup given to all participants; the blood poured out for many; the forgiveness of sins as the cup's covenant-content; the Supper as the new covenant's ongoing ratification-meal

First Corinthians 10:16 — Paul's definition: koinōnia (genuine participation, sharing, communion) in Christ's blood; the cup of blessing is not a bare memorial but a Spirit-mediated real participation in the atonement's benefit

Hebrews 9:20 — the typological lineage: Hebrews quotes Exod 24:8 to describe the Sinai covenant's blood-sprinkling as the type; the antitype is Christ's blood applied through the cup of blessing to the new covenant community

Usage

"First Corinthians 10:16's koinōnia language makes the cup of blessing the primary New Testament text for understanding the Lord's Supper's spiritual character. The cup is not a bare reminder of something that happened once; it is a genuine present participation in the covenant benefit secured by Christ's blood. The believing participant at the Supper is not merely remembering Calvary from a distance; through the Spirit's mediation he or she is genuinely receiving the covenant benefit that Calvary secured."

"Luke 22:20's declaration — “This cup which is poured out for you is the new covenant in My blood” — is the Supper's covenant-renewal charter. Every Supper is a covenant-renewal act: the church gathered around the cup of blessing is re-ratifying its covenant relationship with the God who poured out Christ's blood for its redemption. The Supper is not a ceremony with no ongoing covenant significance; it is the new covenant's regular covenant-renewal meal."

"The communal character of the cup — “Drink from it, all of you” (Matt 26:27) — makes the cup of blessing an act of covenant solidarity. Paul extends this in 1 Corinthians 10:17: “Since there is one bread, we who are many are one body; for we all partake of the one bread.” The cup creates and declares a unity among its participants as sharers in the one blood; to drink it in an unworthy manner (1 Cor 11:27–29) is to make a false covenant claim about belonging to the body of Christ."
